content: 1. Feeding of newborns was encouraged either through gavage or cup feeding, or by breastfeeding. Early initiation and gradual escalation of feeds were promoted to minimize the reliance on intravenous fluids. 2. Monitoring for hypoglycemia was emphasized, with staff being trained to detect and address hypoglycemic episodes promptly by monitoring blood glucose levels. 3. Infection prevention and management were prioritized. This included strict hand hygiene protocols, such as washing hands upon entering the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) and sanitizing hands between contact with different infants. The use of disposable materials was encouraged wherever feasible. Staff were trained to identify signs of infection and potential sepsis, and antibiotic stewardship was promoted within the neonatal unit. 4. Kangaroo mother care (KMC) was recommended for all preterm and low birth weight infants. In some hospitals, dedicated rooms adjacent to the neonatal care unit were made available to facilitate this care. 5. In most hospitals, surfactant therapy and mechanical ventilation were not available for managing preterm infants. These interventions were also not part of the respiratory support provided during the trial. 6. Adequate funding and budget allocation were necessary to ensure the continuous procurement and distribution of antenatal corticosteroids. These medications needed to be readily available in antenatal, labor, and emergency obstetric wards. Simplified administration protocols and standardized communication regarding dosing and administration during handovers and referrals were also essential. 7. Local guidelines and clinical protocols were adapted through a multi-stakeholder, consensus-driven process. These guidelines were aligned with WHO, national, sub-national, and facility-level recommendations. National guidelines included clear criteria for the appropriate use and acceptable regimens of antenatal corticosteroids, addressing specific conditions such as diabetes or fetal growth restriction. 8. Training for healthcare professionals was emphasized in several areas, including the safe and appropriate use of antenatal corticosteroids, gestational age dating using ultrasound, and preterm newborn care (e.g., resuscitation, oxygen therapy, CPAP, thermal care, breastfeeding, blood glucose monitoring, infection prevention and management, and kangaroo mother care). 9. Reminder systems, educational materials, and decision aids were made accessible to healthcare professionals. Key performance indicators, audits, and feedback mechanisms were also implemented to monitor the use of antenatal corticosteroids. 10. Change champions or opinion leaders were appointed to promote the appropriate use of antenatal corticosteroids. 11. Effective implementation of these recommendations required reorganization of care and redistribution of healthcare resources, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. This included ensuring the availability of respiratory support (e.g., CPAP, intubation, oxygen therapy) and addressing challenges such as uncertainty in gestational age estimation and lack of effective referral mechanisms. 12. Local protocols were developed to integrate the management of women at high risk of preterm birth and preterm newborns within a continuum of care, considering contextual factors influencing preterm newborn survival. 13. Accurate pregnancy dating using the best available methods during early antenatal care visits was emphasized. Healthcare staff were trained to estimate gestational age and recognize clinical features of spontaneous preterm labor. 14. Local arrangements were made to ensure consistent supplies of antenatal corticosteroids (dexamethasone or betamethasone) in appropriate dose vials. 15. Other aspects of maternal and newborn care quality were considered, including the provision of radiant warmers and kangaroo mother care for preterm newborns. 16. Clear referral pathways for women at high risk of preterm birth were established within healthcare facilities. 17. The implementation and impact of these recommendations were monitored at health-service, regional, and country levels using clearly defined criteria and indicators aligned with locally agreed targets. 18. Data on the implementation of these recommendations were collected and evaluated in collaboration with WHO monitoring and evaluation teams. This data was used to assess the impact on national policies in WHO Member States. 19. Interrupted time series, clinical audits, or criterion-based clinical audits were suggested as methods to gather relevant data on antenatal corticosteroid therapy. 20. Clearly defined review criteria and indicators were needed, which could be associated with locally agreed targets. Indicators included coverage, effective coverage (quality), effectiveness (impact on neonatal outcomes), and safety of antenatal corticosteroid therapy. 21. Research priorities were identified to address knowledge gaps, including factors affecting the use and scale-up of antenatal corticosteroids in lowand middle-income countries, benefits and risks of use in specific gestational age ranges, and strategies to optimize implementation and equitable distribution of benefits. 22. Long-term outcomes of infants exposed to antenatal corticosteroids, including those born at term, were highlighted as an area requiring further research. 23. The minimum effective dose of antenatal corticosteroid therapy and the optimal administration-to-birth interval were identified as critical research questions. 24. Strategies to support shared decision-making between women, their families, and healthcare providers regarding antenatal corticosteroid use were emphasized. 25. The benefits and risks of antenatal corticosteroids among women with multiple pregnancies at risk of preterm birth were also identified as a research priority. 26. WHO regularly reviews its maternal and perinatal health recommendations to prioritize new and existing questions for development and updating. Recommendations are updated when new evidence potentially impacts the current evidence base. Concerns about the validity of recommendations should be promptly communicated to guideline implementers.
